utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: Good morning, everyone. Mr. Milovancevic, I believe you were in the thick of cross-examination of the witness, Ambassador Galbraith.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Ambassador. We will now proceed with your cross-examination. Yesterday we left it off with some questions about the shelling of Zagreb. To the extent possible, pursuant to the rules that exist here at the Tribunal, let us go back to the moment when you explained why you considered the Republic of Srpska Krajina the so-called Srpska Krajina and you said it was because it was a self-proclaimed republic that nobody in the world recognised as such. In this regard I would like to ask you as follows: Is it true that in 1991, before the arrival of UNPROFOR and its deployment, Republika Srpska Krajina had its own territory? Is that true?

utterances.speaker: PETER GALBRAITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Since there was no Republika Srpska Krajina, one cannot speak of it as having territory. There was territory under the control of local Serb authorities, paramilitaries, but that doesn't make it the territory of a state.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Was this a territory at which the Serb population was a majority or a minority in Croatia, and what territory was it where the United Nations deployed their forces in order to keep peace and in order to peacefully resolve the Yugoslav crisis? Is this the territory that we are referring to?

utterances.speaker: PETER GALBRAITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Before the war, some of the territory in question had had a Serbian majority. Some of it had had a Croatian majority. As a result of the activities conducted by in part by your client, the ethnic cleansing of the Croatian population, the territory was by the end of 1991 almost purely Serbian.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: In that territory that we are talking about now, were there bodies of the Serb authorities so to speak, the president of the republic, the government of Republika Srpska Krajina, the assembly of the Republika Srpska Krajina? Are you familiar with that? Are you aware of that?

utterances.speaker: PETER GALBRAITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were bodies that said that they had those titles. Nobody recognised them as lawful authorities but they did exercise de facto control over the territory, and we met with the leaders of these de facto bodies.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Am I right in saying that in that territory, the authorities of the Republic of Croatia had no power, had no control whatsoever, at that time, in 1991?

utterances.speaker: PETER GALBRAITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. They had no actual power on the ground because it was occupied or controlled by the rebel Serb authorities supported by Serbia.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: This territory had its population, its territory, and its bodies of power elected in elections and you call it the so-called republic. Can you by the same token call the Republic of Croatia the so-called Republic of Croatia?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Milovancevic, Mr. Whiting is on his feet.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Well, I was going to make an objection but I'll withdraw it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: Thank you. Please continue, Mr. Milovancevic. Counsel has withdrawn his objection.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Can you answer my question, Mr. Ambassador?

utterances.speaker: PETER GALBRAITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, technically speaking, anybody or anything can be so-called, but even something that's lawful is so-called. I'm so-called Peter Galbraith. But the Republic of Croatia was an entity that existed within the former Yugoslavia and it became a -- when Yugoslavia dissolved at the end of 1991, it became a legally recognised successor state, a member of the United Nations recognised by most countries in the world.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Are you aware of the fact that the Republika Srpska Krajina asked for international recognition and do you know whether it received international recognition, if it did?

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Okay, now I am going to object. I think that these questions this morning first of all they go beyond scope of direct. We are talking now about a time period that the witness specifically did not testify about. Secondly, the witness was the Ambassador to Croatia starting in 1993 and these questions are all about 1991.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: Mr. Milovancevic, what do you have to say in response?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My questions have to do with the Prosecutor's examination-in-chief. He did ask the Ambassador about Republika Srpska Krajina and I just want to know why he called it a so-called republic. It exists, it has existed since 1991. Therefore, my questions have to do with the period that was referred to by the Prosecutor in his questions to the witness, when he called for his opinion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: Very well, but the point that is being taken is that the period in respect of which the legality is in issue is the later period and not the earlier period that you're referring to. Therefore, it's outside of the phase that was dealt with in direct or examination-in-chief by the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, in order to avoid misunderstanding and not to break the rules, the essence of my questions has to do with the facts and the facts have to do with the legality. The Prosecutor raised the issue of legality and asked the Ambassador to provide his opinion on the status of the RSK. However, I can move on. I have received enough answers from the Ambassador, if you agree with that, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Whiting.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Your Honour, I appreciate that and -- that resolution of the issue. But I do want to clarify one thing, and that is that I don't believe that I asked any questions of the witness about issues of legality. They were factual issues about why the entity was called the so-called RSK but I didn't -- this witness is not here as a legal expert and I have not tried to draw legal opinions from him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: No. That is correct, but he has himself given certain evidence and that evidence has indicated that he did not believe that at the relevant time it was an entity that had the lawful sanction from the international community. So I think in that regard, counsel is entitled to put questions to him concerning the issue of whether there was recognition, the issue of legality, but it must be contained to the period that was referred to during the course of examination-in-chief.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Yes. I fully agree with that, Your Honour. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Milovancevic, you have heard what the Chamber has said. Please proceed. But I believe that the question has effectively been answered by the witness. If you have a different position to put to him, put it directly instead of circuitously in relation to the relevant period. Remember, this is not only a witness in respect of which the regular guidelines of the Chamber exist but he himself has certain protective measures which were referred to initially that touch and concern him and how he can be examined and cross-examined.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. I have finished with that topic and I will indeed proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: At one point in answering the Prosecutor's questions, you said, Mr. Ambassador, that Milosevic had told you that he would not accept the plan and that he would not receive the Z-4 plan delegation. With that regard, I would like to know whether you received that information from Mr. Milosevic personally. If not, who was it who told you that?

utterances.speaker: PETER GALBRAITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not receive the message -- I did not receive the message from Milosevic personally, since the message was that he would not receive the Z-4 delegation. I think the -- this was conveyed through the co-chairman of ICFY as well as the American embassy in Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: I would like to remind you of the fact that yesterday you referred to a report that was sent by the British embassy on the 3rd of August 1995 and in that letter your meeting with Mr. Babic is described and it contains a statement saying that the American embassy in Belgrade had been in contact with Mr. Milosevic, however this was not correct. You believed that they were in contact with Mr. Milosevic. However it turned out that they couldn't get in touch with him. I would like to know based on which information were you able to convey the information about the meeting with Mr. Babic on the 2nd and the 3rd of August and how did you know that Mr. Milosevic had been informed about the Z-4 plan, or were those just your assumptions?

utterances.speaker: PETER GALBRAITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, with regard to the meeting with Mr. Babic, I personally had the meeting with Mr. Babic so I knew everything that had transpired in that meeting. It was a meeting between just the two of us, plus an interpreter and a -- and my assistant, in the American embassy in Belgrade. And I and my assistant prepared the reports on that meeting. As to whether Milosevic was informed of the Z-4 plan, the plan was well known in -- at the time. It was in the press. Copies of it were published after it was presented. So I'm sure that he did in fact know what the contents of the Z-4 plan were.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can one say that in such a situation, the one that you have just explained, the information conveyed to the Ambassadors of the contact group, the Ambassadors of Spain, Italy and Canada, the information that speaks about your meeting with Mr. Babic on the 2nd and 3rd of August 1995, is the information about the embassy of America in Belgrade having informed Mr. Milosevic was actually an arbitrary piece of information, because that meeting had actually never taken place?

utterances.speaker: PETER GALBRAITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Ambassador Hewitt's cable accurately reflected the content of my meeting with Mr. Babic, which I had briefed to the contact group plus the additional Ambassadors that you mentioned. I said that the American embassy was or would be briefing Milosevic or would be seeing him to solicit his support. That was what I believed to be the case, since our charge, Rudi Perina, had instructions from the State Department to go see Milosevic and to brief him. I, however, had left Belgrade in the morning of the 3rd and this meeting with the Ambassadors was shortly after I had arrived back in Zagreb, and I did not know at that time that this briefing was not going to take place. If Gavin Hewitt had asked me at 6 p.m. that evening, I think I would have known that Milosevic had in fact not seen Perina and then his cable would have been a little bit different but I don't think that there is any significance at all to the fact that I thought at 2.00 or whatever time it was in the afternoon that that briefing was going to go ahead.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: Ambassador, before the next question comes, may I ask for clarification, before you mentioned that the message of Mr. Milosevic in your eyes has been conveyed through the co-chairman of ICFY as well as through the American embassy. What is ICFY? What abbreviation is that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It is the International Conference for the Former Yugoslavia. It was the -- but just to be clear, Your Honour, I'm referring then to our request that was put forward in January of 1995 to come to Belgrade to present the plan. The original idea is that the Z-4 peace plan would be presented first to Milosevic [sic], second to the leaders of the so-called Republika Srpska Krajina, and then after that we would all go to Belgrade to present it to Milosevic. Milosevic told the co-chairman of ICFY that he would not receive us and the same word was sent to the American embassy in Belgrade to pass on to me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: In other words, you've explained to the honourable judge that the first piece of information on Z-4 dating from January 1995 should have been conveyed to Mr. Milosevic and that's one position. And the telegram and your information about your meeting with Mr. Babic and about an immediate Croatian attack, this second situation refers to the 2nd and 3rd of August of 1995. Have we now been able to clarify that little issue, Mr. Ambassador?

utterances.speaker: PETER GALBRAITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Just to make sure that is no misunderstanding, these are, as you say, two separate events, one related to the presentation of the Z-4 peace plan, and the second related to an agreement that I concluded with Mr. Babic on the evening of the 2nd of August 1995, which involved five points, one of which was that Babic would accept the Z-4 plan with the private message to Tudjman that he understood the end result would be much less autonomy for the RSK than contained in the Z-4 plan. On the 3rd of August, there was a -- the -- Rudi Perina attempted to be in touch with Slobodan Milosevic to get him to support this deal between Babic and myself from the previous night, and that was considered extremely important because Babic had said, "One word from Milosevic, one sentence from Milosevic, and Martic and the other leaders of the RSK will accept this deal that Galbraith and I have concluded."

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you for this clarification, Mr. Ambassador.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: Galbraith and I.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was quoting Babic. I hope I've been clear.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: Right, right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: With regard to this explanation that we have arrived at, and with regard to your words that Milosevic would -- said that he would not accept the Z-4 plan and who you received that information from, you also told us yesterday that Milosevic had accepted the cease-fire but that he was afraid of the offer of the autonomy because of Kosovo. Actually he was afraid that such an autonomy would be demanded for Kosovo as well. With this regard I would have a question for you, Mr. Ambassador. Are you familiar with the fact that Kosovo, in 1991 and in 1995, had a full autonomy in the Republic of Serbia?

utterances.speaker: PETER GALBRAITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not aware of that fact because it is not true.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: If you're not aware of something, I don't see how you can claim it to be untrue. However, I have the following question for you concerning Kosovo. Have you ever had a chance to look at the SFRY constitution according to which Kosovo had its autonomy, has its academy, has its own entire schooling system, that's to say education, health system, police, everything. It had the highest form of autonomy under the European standards both in 1991 and in 1995? Now, do you know these things or do you not?

utterances.speaker: PETER GALBRAITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am generally aware of what the constitution of the former Yugoslavia provided and what was intended for Kosovo, but the reality in Kosovo is that the Albanian majority was completely disenfranchised. It was run by Milosevic with the Serbian minority. There was brutal repression in the province. And so it is not possible to speak of meaningful autonomy in Kosovo.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Galbraith, between 1993 and 1998, you were the US Ambassador to Croatia. Now, were you or rather did you visit Kosovo ever before that period and who did you have contacts with and in what way did you obtain the information that you are relaying now? The information you're testifying to now, as a politician?

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: I'd object to the -- I would object to that last reference. He's not testifying as a politician.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: You only object on that issue, the reference to the witness as a politician?

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: You know, I'm also very close to objecting on scope grounds here once again but I think a question about the basis of his knowledge is a fair question --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: -- if it doesn't go further than that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: Mr. Milovancevic -- one moment, please, Ambassador Galbraith. Mr. Milovancevic has to have the opportunity of response. Please do respond, Mr. Milovancevic. Or do you concede that your description by use of the word "politician" as ascribed to the witness was somewhat inappropriate?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, if the latter part of my question is objectionable, then I will withdraw it. What I wanted to say was that Mr. Galbraith is an Ambassador, must have been a man who was involved in politics and I do consider him a man involved in politics and therefore a politician. However, I can fully withdraw that part of my question, if that poses a problem.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: From my knowledge of that state, it does not follow. Please go ahead.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I visited Kosovo twice, in 1990 -- December of 1991 and November of 1992. I met with the local Serbian authorities, including the head of the autonomous region, as well as the Ibrahim Rugova and the Albanian democratic movement. I might add I visited Kosovo Polje and some of the Serbian monasteries as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: How would that affect the opinion which you formed in respect of that particular state of -- in relation to Kosovo, rather?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was clear from those visits that there was brutal repression of the Albanian majority by the Serbian minority and that there was no meaningful self-rule on the part of the Albanian majority, and therefore it doesn't change my conclusion that one of the reasons that Milosevic did not like the Z-4 plan is that a -- an arrangement that provided very great autonomy to the Serbian minority within Croatia, in the Krajina region, would set a bad precedent for the -- for Kosovo because it would imply that perhaps he would have to grant the same kind of autonomy for the Albanian majority. I might add, Your Honours, that there was also another reason why he didn't like the Z-4 plan, which I should have mentioned yesterday, which is that the plan provided for autonomy for the Serb majority region of Krajina, as I testified yesterday, but it involved the full reintegration into Croatia of those areas, like Eastern Slavonia, which had had a Croatian majority in 1991, and his real interest was in trying to acquire Eastern Slavonia. He didn't care about the Serbian population in Krajina, which was an impoverished region far from Serbia but was much more interested in Eastern Slavonia which was rich farm land and had oil fields.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes, Mr. Milovancevic, please continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: As far as I understood your answer, Mr. Galbraith, you made one visit in 1991 and another one in 1992, the total of two visits to Kosovo. My question in connection with that is as follows. On these occasions, were you visiting Serbia or Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: Mr. Milovancevic, you had been allowed a certain laxity but do remember that there are specific restrictions concerning the witness. And you have to honour them.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. I will move quickly with this topic. I believe we are close to finishing it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Tell us, Mr. Ambassador, you were visiting the area of former Yugoslavia in 1991. Who did you visit specifically on the occasion of your visit to Kosovo in 1991 and the same question for 1992?

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm going to object. I think the -- I think the witness has addressed the issue. He's given the basis for his opinion, fully explained it. I think this goes far beyond the -- what is fair on cross, given the direct. We are now just entering into all kinds of questions about Kosovo. I would also add, Your Honour, that I would like to while I'm on my feet address the issue of the length of the cross-examination. By my calculation, the cross examination has just exceeded the length of my direct examination and by the Court's order of 13 April 2004 [sic], paragraph 11, the Court ordered that ordinarily cross-examination should not exceed the length of direct examination. Of course, I recognise that there are exceptions and I understand if it may have to go on for a little longer but I don't think it should go on for very much longer and in fact in this case the witness does have other arrangements to leave this afternoon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: Well, each counsel has his own style but I'm sure that Mr. Milovancevic will be guided by the fact that there are time limits, in terms of the guidelines. And probably you could give an indication to the Trial Chamber at this point how much longer you intend to be with the witness, having regard to the fact that you have exceeded the cross-examination -- the examination-in-chief. And the guidelines are in fact the 13th of April 2006. We would just like to have it on the record. If there is a reference to 2004, it was an error. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, as for the objection by my learned friend, in order to speed up the examination I'll withdraw my question. We have received appropriate answers any way. First of all to save time, this examination lasted a bit longer precisely because of the numerous objections that consumed practically half of the Defence's cross-examination. I had the intention of not prolonging this examination too far. I will move along quickly. I do have the caution received both by the Chamber and the Prosecution and I will act accordingly. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: I take your point, Mr. Milovancevic, but some of the objections were properly taken. So you have to try to be more direct, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Galbraith, yesterday, after you explained your view of Milosevic's position vis-a-vis the Z-4 plan, you stated that his, that's to say Milosevic's, dream concerning greater Serbia included Slavonia, Krajina and Dubrovnik. My question in connection with this is as follows: Did you ever discuss his dreams with Mr. Milosevic?

utterances.speaker: PETER GALBRAITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: I met with Mr. Milosevic in October of 1992, in Belgrade, and I raised the issue of greater Serbia. He at that time denied that he had any ambitions for greater Serbia but frankly I didn't believe him and I think nobody else in the government -- in the US government believed him either.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Does this mean that despite Mr. Milosevic's denial of the thesis of a greater Serbia, you and the American government were of the view that in fact this idea existed, that's to say that was your position to believe that? Is that what you're saying now?

utterances.speaker: PETER GALBRAITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believed, and I think this view was shared by many people in the US government who've dealt with the Balkans, that Milosevic had a plan for greater Serbia, that he was implementing the plan, that he was using the military forces of the former Yugoslavia to try to accomplish that objective.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: In your testimony in the Milosevic case, when answering the questions by the Prosecutor, you stated that you never saw any documents or anything in writing that would support the idea of greater Serbia; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: PETER GALBRAITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't answer that question because I don't have the testimony in the Milosevic case in front of me, and I would want to see the exact exchange to understand the point that I was making.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Milovancevic, do you have that testimony with you to present to the witness so that he may properly observe what you are putting to him and answer your question appropriately and effectively in the circumstances? The guidelines again are upon you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I'm quite satisfied with Mr. Galbraith's answer. I do not wish to waste any more time on this. I find the explanation quite satisfactory by your leave.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Galbraith, yesterday you spoke of Mr. Milosevic's dreams of greater Serbia. Also in response to the Prosecutor's question, you presented, or rather gave some statements concerning Mr. Martic which not only went beyond what is propriety but rather went to directly offend him, that he was a man of limited abilities, of limited intelligence. I'm interested in the following. The disagreement of Mr. Martic with your political proposals and views, was that the basis for your assessment of him?

utterances.speaker: PETER GALBRAITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Let me begin by saying that it was not my intention to offend the accused. I was asked by the Prosecution for my assessment of him, as I had been asked in the Milosevic trial, and I gave the same answer. My assessment was based on the meetings I had with him, as well as conversations I had with other people who knew him and had interacted with him. I felt that he was a man of very limited abilities, was way over his head in trying to handle the situation of the Krajina Serbs, and frankly, yes, I think it was an act of extraordinary stupidity to have refused a peace plan, refused to receive a peace plan that came from the most powerful countries in the world, a peace plan that had it been implemented, had the negotiations proceeded, there would have been no Operation Storm, the population, the Serbian population of the Krajina would have remained, the -- there would have been very substantial self-government there, and quite possibly the defendant would not be here in this courtroom.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Galbraith, yesterday you explained that Mr. Martic's objection was that he could not discuss the Z-4 plan until a decision is taken to extend the mandate of UNPROFOR in Croatia and that this was in fact done in the month of March. In connection with this, did the attack by the Croatian forces against the UN zone in Western Slavonia, therefore a protected area, at the point in time when you were proposing a peace plan, give the basis for Mr. Martic to believe that this was a bona fide plan that was able to give any hope to the Krajina population?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: Can the witness properly answer for Mr. Martic in that regard? Is it a fair question to put to the witness, do you think?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I will rephrase the question. This will be a direct question for Mr. Galbraith.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Your negotiating intentions, both of you and those who authored the Z-4, plan, were they sincere in their approach to the Krajina Serb people, where in the midst of a peace process, the Croatian authorities wipe out the entire Western Slavonia area without any consequences to follow?

utterances.speaker: PETER GALBRAITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can say to you that the United States, the Russian Federation, the European Union and the United Nations, all of whom were co-sponsors of the Z-4 plan were very sincere in wanting to find a peaceful settlement to the conflict within Croatia that provided very substantial autonomy for the Serbian people and also enabled those who had been displaced or ethnically cleansed to return to our homes -- to their homes. We devoted enormous effort, time and effort, to this process. I can tell you that to this day I am bitterly disappointed that it was unsuccessful. When you refuse to negotiate peace seriously, war often is the consequence. Mr. Martic played games in 1994 that prevented the peace process from going forward. He refused the plan on January 30th, 1995. The direct consequence of his action was the operation that took place in Western Slavonia. He demonstrated fully in that operation that he had no ability, the RSK had no ability to defend themselves and, of course, the Croatians then were emboldened to launch Operation Storm in August of 1995. All of this was a huge tragedy for the people of the Krajina and it's something that I personally deeply regret and I think that's true of the others who participated in this peace process.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Ambassador, you said that the greatest powers of the world were there to give an offer to the Krajina Serb people. On the other hand, you tell us that the Croatian authorities did what they willed. Did you have the abilities, were you able to stop the Croatian authorities from engaging in these operations? You were there, offering a peace settlement in Krajina, reportedly, while at the same time, although the Croatian authorities should find themselves content with the peace process, they launch an attack against Western Slavonia. Did you have any influence to wield on the Croatian authorities?

utterances.speaker: PETER GALBRAITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: We had substantial influence on the Croatian authorities, and we urged them successfully urged them to exercise restraint on a number of occasions in 1993. In November 1994, when the RSK was attacking across the international border into the Bihac enclave, we put a lot of pressure on the Croatians to exercise restraint. The fact is, because of your client, there was no peace process in April of 1995. We had presented the plan or attempted to present the plan in January of 1995. He refused physically to pick up the plan, to touch it. And after that, there really wasn't a peace process. The Croatians were frustrated. He then refused to keep the agreements that he had already made, include -- he closed the highway through Western Slavonia. War is the consequence of what happens when you don't make peace. And it was an avoidable tragedy.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Ambassador, my next question has to do with the period immediately preceding your talks with Mr. Babic, which took place on the 2nd and 3rd of August 1995. In response to Amicus Tapuskovic in the Milosevic's case, that is to say Amicus Tapuskovic's questions, you said that you were at Brioni on the 30th and 31st of June. Was that indeed -- or rather, July. Was that indeed the case, Mr. Galbraith? Were you at Brioni?

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Your Honour, I wonder first if we could have a reference for my own purposes. Again, there is -- if the witness could have available to him the prior testimony.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Milovancevic. Do you have that which is necessary?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour. I'm simply trying to proceed more quickly with the witness. We have all seen the material but I'd like to know whether Mr. Galbraith was at Brioni on the 30th or the 31st of July 1995. This is a question which doesn't have to do with any document.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Your Honour, but --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: The foundation for the question is contained in a document.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Yes, and in fact I have now found the reference and in fact the witness -- the counsel has misstated the evidence that was given in the testimony. On page 78, 26th of June 2003, the Ambassador stated that he was there on the 1st of August 1995, and in this context, it's an extremely important distinction. So this is precisely why it's important to have the document available.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Milovancevic, have you heard what Mr. Whiting has said as to the de facto evidence that was given? That it is in fact a reference to the 1st of August? And could you give the witness the opportunity to answer the question in respect of what was said and then to go on to the second part of it?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, my question is a general question, whether the witness remembers having had a meeting with President Tudjman on the eve of the Operation Storm, whether it was in July or in August 1995. It's a general question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: So you withdraw your reference to the evidence that was given in the other case, then?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That is correct, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: Very well. Please go ahead.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation].

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Do you know that before your meeting with Mr. Tudjman, towards the end of July or maybe on the 1st day of August 1995, there was an operation by the Croatian armed forces in Grahovo and in Glamoc and these are places in the territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina. The Croatian armed forces took those two places in the territory of Bosnia and Herzegovina? Are you familiar with that fact?

utterances.speaker: PETER GALBRAITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: You've also explained that around the 21st of July 1995, you learned about the Croatian intention to launch a military intervention in Krajina. With regard to that, I'm interested in the part of the answer that you provided saying that the government of the United States was in two mind as to what to do because they feared a possible outcome of the situation in Bihac. Are you familiar with what the real situation in Bihac was at the time, Mr. Galbraith?

utterances.speaker: PETER GALBRAITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I was familiar with the situation in Bihac, but I did not say that the United States was of two minds. We had a very clear position.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Do you know that before Operation Storm, Mr. Thorvald Stoltenberg the co-chairman of the conference on Yugoslavia and Mr. Akashi the Serb forces had withdrawn from Bihac and all the military activity had ceased and this was done with the mediation of the two gentlemen that I mentioned?

utterances.speaker: PETER GALBRAITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: The situation in the two weeks before Operation Storm was very complicated. There was an attack by the Bosnian Serb army and the army of the Republika Srpska Krajina on the Bihac enclave, the army of the ARSK crossing the international border. There was a time when we feared that Bihac would fall and that Ratko Mladic would engage in the same kind of slaughter of the people of Bihac, the men and boys of Bihac, that he had done in Srebrenica. In the few days immediately before Operation Storm, there were indications that the forces from the ARSK were ceasing their military operations, but at that stage, the momentum for war was very strong and as I've explained, we did attempt even at that late stage to try to find a peaceful settlement.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Galbraith, are you familiar with the presidential statement of the Security Council of the United Nations dating from February 1994, in which the Croatian forces were requested to withdraw from Bosnia-Herzegovina, from the territory of a different state? With regard to this, do you find that the operations in Glamoc and Grahovo meant that Croatia had again intervened on the territory of a different state despite the previous warnings on the eve of Operation Storm and flash? Is that the momentum that you were referring to, Mr. Galbraith?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Whiting?

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. I'm going to object on relevance grounds. I don't see how this would be relevant.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: Mr. Milovancevic, what is your response? I was making the same inquiries.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, the witness has told us that the Croatian side used the situation in Bihac as a pretext to launch an operation on the territory of Krajina and that his government had taken a position on that. What I want to know is whether this witness's government thought that the intervention of the Croatian troops in the territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina regarded as illegal and contrary to the international law. This was in preparation of operations of storm and flash. The burden here is transferred on to Mr. Martic, and Knin fell after the Croatian troops had taken Glamoc because it is from Glamoc that the Croatian artillery was able to shell Knin and this is what the Trial Chamber should be aware of. And this is why I have put this question to the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Your Honour, I think counsel has explained the question and what it is he's trying to elicit but I don't think he's explained the relevance of it. I don't see how that information is relevant to the charges and the indictment in the case before the Trial Chamber.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: I crave your indulgence.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I would like to move on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Milovancevic, might I just say something? It sounds very much like it is material that you would address the Chamber on when the relevant time comes. But for now, the direct relevance, I do not see it. So yes, please move on.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Galbraith, did you hear anything about the meeting between Mr. Tudjman and the top leadership, military leadership of Croatia on the eve of Operation Storm on the 30th or the 31st of July 1995? At that meeting he informed his military leadership he -- that there was no military justification for the operation against the Serbs, i.e. that Bihac could not be taken as a pretext? However, that the Republic of Croatia enjoyed the support of the government of the USA if it intervened in Western Slavonia? Are you familiar with that? Are you aware of that speech that Mr. Tudjman delivered to his military leadership?

utterances.speaker: PETER GALBRAITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: If I may ask a question, are you referring to the transcript of the meeting in Brioni, I believe on the 31st of July, that was subsequently made public by the Croatian government?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: PETER GALBRAITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Obviously I was not aware of that -- of any speech that he made to his military commanders in a closed meeting at the time, but I did see the transcript at the time of the Milosevic trial.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Yesterday on direct you said that Mr. Babic after the meeting with yourself --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: I needs a clarification from the witness. Before you proceed, might I get a clarification? When you answer yes, Mr. Witness, are you referring to yes you're aware of that meeting, or are you answering yes to the statement that was made? Are you adopting that as a statement that was made within the confines of the transcript on that occasion?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour, for the clarification which I should have made. I'm answering yes that I'm aware that there was a transcript of the meeting. If the transcript were presented to me and I sat here and read it I might be able to agree or disagree with a characterisation of it but I'm not agreeing with any characterisation of it right now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: Would you have the transcript? Is it necessary for you to produce it, Mr. Milovancevic, if you might stand? Thank you. Are you pursuing the contents of the transcript?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I do have the contents of the transcript, but I believe that at this point it is not important for the witness because he was not present at the meeting and he said that he read about it in the press. That's why I'm not presenting the witness with the transcript. At the Milosevic trial, he was familiarised with the contents of the transcript and I'm not insisting on that particular detail at this moment. Thank you very much. And I believe this is a good time for our break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: Would you be much longer?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. I'm sure I'll be able to finish in the course of the next session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Milovancevic. We will take a break and come back at quarter to 11.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Milovancevic?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Galbraith, we finished the last session by talking about the meeting with Mr. Tudjman and his meeting with the top military leadership of the 31st July, on the eve of Operation Storm. You said that at the Milosevic trial you were presented with a transcript from that meeting on the 31st of July. Do you remember whether you were asked questions by Mr. Tapuskovic on page 23200 on 26th of July, questions about Tudjman having as a goal of that meeting to strike a final blow on Serbs so that they could disappear and he gave a task to Mr. Sarinic to go to Geneva and negotiate but just to buy time because he did not intend to sign any agreements? Do you remember that detail? If not, you can tell us so?

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Your Honour, could the witness once again could the witness be presented with the transcript because again there has been a reference to it?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Milovancevic, before the break you were asked about the transcript. Do you have the transcript? Please produce it to the witness and have him look at it and proceed on that foundation.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour; I understand your comment. Given the witness's previous answer the Prosecutor's objection, I'm not going to proceed. I will move on in order to avoid wasting any more time on this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: You won't be wasting time. You'll be doing what is necessary and abiding by the guidelines. It's not a question of whether or not you're wasting time here.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, the question was not direct. That's why I'm not insisting on the transcript and on this evidence because the witness did not attend that meeting. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Galbraith, do you know anything about the fact that Mr. -- Secretariat General of the United Nations, and I believe that at the time that was Mr. Boutros-Ghali, on the 3rd of August 1995, which is on the eve of Operation Storm, he called Mr. Tudjman and implored with him not to launch any military operations against Krajina? Do you know anything about that detail at all?

utterances.speaker: PETER GALBRAITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: At the present time, I don't recall the specifics of that. We -- there were a number of people, myself included, who urged President Tudjman not to take military action on the 3rd of August. I've already testified to that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: On the 4th of August 1995, the Republic of Croatia launched a large-scale military operation against the RSK, against the zones under the protection of the United Nations. A few days later, the entire territory was occupied, the population was expelled, and the property of the Serb population there was destroyed. With regard to that, I have the following question. Are you familiar with the fact that the world media published your photo on a tank of the Croatian army, a photo that was taken during Operation Storm?

utterances.speaker: PETER GALBRAITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: No photograph was taken of me during Operation Storm on a Croatian tank. I was not on a Croatian tank during Operation Storm. The only photograph that was taken in fact was on a tractor with Serbian refugees who I was trying to protect from a Croatian mob, as you know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: Successfully or unsuccessfully?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Successfully.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Milovancevic your client is asked to contain himself and behave appropriately unless he has some communication to make to you in the course of this hearing.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I wish to say something, of course, I do.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: Communication can only be made through your counsel.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, may I have a brief moment with my client?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: You wish the benefit of an audience with him, with your client?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just for a moment, thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: Very briefly, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: You're welcome.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] With your leave I would like to proceed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: Would you have the photograph of the witness on the tractor with you to place before him? No?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There is even a video clip, Your Honour, featuring Mr. Galbraith on a tractor, but there is no dispute about that. Mr. Galbraith was indeed on a tractor with the Serb refugees and he was helping the population and protect the population from being stoned by a mob. But this was not my question. I only asked Mr. Ambassador whether he was on a Croatian armoured vehicle? We received an answer and I am happy with that answer. I have nothing further to that effect.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: My following question --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: I'm sorry, the witness on a tank, not on a tractor, because what is in issue is the fact that he was not on a tank, he was on a tractor? So I correct myself. Do you have the photograph of him on the tank? Would your response be the same?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, at this moment, the Defence team does not consider this photo important. We will try to lead this evidence with other witnesses in different ways. I just wanted to hear from the witness whether he knows anything about that or not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: Very well. Yes, Mr. Whiting?

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Your Honour, I don't want to waste time but I think that there -- I'm not clear, because counsel needs to have a basis for putting that kind of question to the witness and does he in fact have a photograph that -- as he has described? I would ask that if the Court could get an answer to that question from the counsel to determine if there it was a basis for that question. Because I'm not aware of such a photograph.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: That was what I was attempting to do, particularly by virtue of the fact that Ambassador Galbraith has denied the fact that he was on a tank. He has said where he was and what he was doing and I wanted to be advised as to whether Mr. Milovancevic had that photograph to put to the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, with your leave I would like to explain and I would like to answer my learned friend. In the Milosevic case, Mr. Galbraith explained how he had arrived at the place of combat and he said that he had been in a Croatian armoured vehicle and then that he moved on to a Croatian tractor belonging to a man that he knew, and my question arises from the Milosevic case transcript but I wouldn't waste any more time on that because there will be more time to dwell upon that issue if the Defence team deems the issue to be important, and of some consideration in the course of this trial. And with your leave I would like to proceed with some other questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: Please do. It's just that you had raised the issue yourself in the course of your cross-examination, and I do believe that the witness has something to say. Please go ahead.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: What I -- I arrived at the scene in my armoured car. It was an American automobile that had -- that was armoured. It was a Chevrolet Caprice, not a military vehicle of any kind, and what I testified to is that my original plan was to ride in the convoy of refugees in that vehicle with the American flag flying so that there would be a clear warning to the mob and to the Croatian police that if they were throwing stones at the -- if they allowed stones to be thrown at the refugees they would also be stoning an American -- official American vehicle, in fact the Ambassador's vehicle. I had also told the Croatian President Tudjman that I intended to do this because I was dissatisfied that he had -- that the Croatian government had not protected the refugees. Instead, because a man in the crowd on a tractor recognised me and as I was talking to him - I didn't know him, he recognised me from television - he invited me to ride on his tractor and I decided to do that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes, Mr. Milovancevic. Please proceed. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: In connection with this detail you just mentioned, Mr. Galbraith, about the conduct of the mob, as you put it, and the fact that you put President Tudjman on notice about this, can you describe for us the conduct of the Croatian armed forces in the course of and in the aftermath of Operation Storm vis-a-vis the population, the local population and the property in the area covered by Operation Storm?

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Objection, Your Honour. I would object, Your Honour. The question --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: The question -- we are now moving into the conduct of the Croatian armed forces during the course of Operation Storm. This is, number 1, beyond the scope of direct examination, number 2 it is not relevant.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Milovancevic?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I'm merely trying to arrive at the information about the true intentions and goals of the operation undertaken by the Croatian forces and of Operation Storm through this witness's answers. He told us that the immediate motive of the attack was the Bihac operation. However, before Operation Storm we had Operation Flash, and then we heard about the witness's activities prior to Operation Storm and since he was the eyewitness of all these events that transpired in the course of several days, the 3rd, the 4th and 5th of August 1995, I thought the question relevant in order to hear what the witness had to say about the actual intentions and goals of the Croatian forces, on the one hand, and of the Z-4 plan and of the negotiators on the other side. This might be prejudicial for or damaging for the Prosecution but my intention was not to break the rules. Rather, I wanted to examine the witness on these specific matters.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: The witness spoke in general terms, and I believe that you are going beyond the bound of the rules in seeking to go into these specific areas, and I am not going to allow you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, the problem that the Defence has been constantly faced with in the course of this cross-examination was the attempt by the Prosecution to protect the interests of one state. In the view of the Defence, such an attempt seems to be more important or seems to override the interests of our client and under such circumstances, we are unable to perform our duties properly. We can simply have those questions allowed that suit the Prosecution. I'm afraid I cannot continue with my cross-examination and for these reasons I will have to stop.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: Mr. Milovancevic, please, please, because you're imputing something to the Bench that does not exist, firstly, and there is also the issue concerning the OTP, the conduct of its case, and imputation in respect of the integrity of this witness. Now, are you saying that Mr. Whiting has been in favour and pursuing the interest of one state or are you referring to the evidence of the witness? Or is it both?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, the problem experienced by the Defence is as follows: The Prosecution has called a witness who was an Ambassador of the greatest world power, who testified or rather who witnessed the events in 1995 up to Operation Storm. However, the Defence was allowed to put only a fraction of questions that were completely out of any relevant context. We were prevented from examining the witness properly. Now, this approach by the Prosecution to have the witness examined while protecting the interests of one state, in our view, violates the right to a fair trial. The need to protect these interests is in direct conflict with the need to protect the right to a fair trial. I cannot put a single question that would open up enough space for me to put follow-up questions that I believe are relevant for the case and for my client. This, Your Honour, was not an objection that I raised with regard to this honourable Chamber but with regard to the Prosecution and their course of proceeding. Now, if the need to protect the interests of a state overrides the interests or rather the right to a fair trial, then I no longer wish to continue examining the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: Mr. Milovancevic, I can say this. I'm truly disappointed in you, as you stand there and as I sit here, and if you are imputing in any way that by reason of the fact that this witness is an ambassador of a world power it would affect the manner in which evidence would be dealt with, then that is a very, very sad and inappropriate statement to make. It's also a false statement. He ranks as any other witness in the eyes of the Chamber. And his evidence would be dealt with in the same way as any other witness whatever his or her status. And that is a real and proper fact that you will have to contend with, whether you like it or not. Now, let me say this to you also: The evidence comes before the Chamber with two considerations: A, the guidelines which you would wish to wipe away and have disappear magically. Secondly, there is the issue of the order touching and concerning the witness. I repeat, which dictates in very strong terms how you may question the witness. Can you go beyond direct examination or what I would term examination-in-chief? The answer is in the negative, which you must comprehend. We are also dealing with a particular period, and circumstances in a particular way. And you have been able to accept that. If it is that this witness has given evidence in a manner that in the Defence opinion appears to favour Croatia or any other party, it is open to you to put the reverse position to the witness but in the proper terms, and you are -- I say this as a position coming from 34 years as Defence counsel. If you have the evidence that is contrary to the witness's, put it to the witness in the proper form in cross-examination and if it happens that a case has been made out when the time comes, put your evidence to confront it and to contradict it. I would like to think that in a moment of folly, and in a moment of weakness, you questioned the integrity of the Court, although you claim that it was not directed at the Court, and I think unfairly, Mr. Whiting and the witness, because he was merely attempting to do his duty, as the Bench is, and the witness may give his evidence as it sees it. He's not obliged to agree with the case for the Defence. And I would like you to complete your cross-examination and behave appropriately. If you have finished it, then so let it be, but as for taking your seat in a huff because you didn't get your way, it smacks of being a little bit unfair to all the parties here and somewhat puerile. Please forgive me. You may continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I understand. Your Honour, thank you for cautioning me and I wish to say one more thing only. The position I presented, I presented precisely having regard to the order which has to do with this witness. It was precisely about this order that my objection had to do with. At this moment, I have no further questions for the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Your Honour, I just have very few, maybe two or three questions on redirect. For the first question if we could have Exhibit 391 published, please, on the monitor?

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: If we could go to the second page, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Ambassador, you recognise this as the code cable that you talked about, you testified about earlier?

utterances.speaker: PETER GALBRAITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: I want to ask you about point 4, specifically the source of the information in that point, if you know it. It says, "Babic, who remained calm throughout, apologised for the way the RSK authorities had reacted to the Z-4 plan. He himself had wanted to accept what was on offer." This is the next sentence that I'm interested in. "Martic and Milosevic were opposed." Now, are you able to tell us what the source is for that sentence in the code cable, please?

utterances.speaker: PETER GALBRAITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe. It's Milan Babic.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And did he give that information to you in your meeting with him on August 2nd, 1995?

utterances.speaker: PETER GALBRAITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: He did.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: My only other question is to clear up what may have been a misspeak and I just would refer to page 8 of today's transcript. I just want to read you a sentence of an answer that you gave and ask you if it's accurate. It's in reference to the presentation of the Z-4 plan in January of 1995 and this is what you said, according to the transcript, "The original idea is that the Z-4 peace plan would be presented first to Milosevic, second to the leaders of the so-called Republika Srpska Krajina, and then after that we would all go to Belgrade to present it to Milosevic."

utterances.speaker: PETER GALBRAITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that is an error of the transcript and not of how I spoke.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Could you just it's just for purposes of the record if you could clarify?

utterances.speaker: PETER GALBRAITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. What I said was that the plan -- the original idea was that the plan would be first presented to President Tudjman in Zagreb, then to the leaders of the so-called RSK in Knin, and finally to Milosevic in Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Thank you, Ambassador. Those are all my questions, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Judge Hoepfel, are there any questions you wish to put to the witness?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: No questions, thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: I just have one or two questions. You were cross-examined concerning a statement made by the accused, Mr. Martic, that he was sorry about the shelling of Zagreb and he had in fact been aiming for military targets. You recall that evidence?

utterances.speaker: PETER GALBRAITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The article by John Pomfritt in the Washington Post.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: Now, what I want to get from you, and please tell me if you're in a position to speak to this fact, where would the nearest military target have been? If you do not know, then just say so.

utterances.speaker: PETER GALBRAITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't speak to the precise distance, but the Ministry of Defence was several kilometres away. But aside from that, if you -- if one considers that a military target, there were no military targets in downtown Zagreb. It was a -- the centre of a city, purely a civilian area.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: Thank you. And now another question. You were asked about the normality, having regard to diplomatic protocol, of attending on and conferring on a weekly and daily basis with the Croatian president. What circumstances that you spoke to prompted this?

utterances.speaker: PETER GALBRAITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm afraid, Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: You did say in answer to him when you were asked if it were normal for you to do that as a diplomat, given the diplomatic protocol of having the monthly and weekly meetings and being in such close association, as I recall the evidence, with the Croatian president, and you said the circumstances would dictate how often you met with the person and how you communicate with the person and I'm asking what were the specific circumstances in this instance that prompted you to meet in that fashion and to communicate in that fashion?

utterances.speaker: PETER GALBRAITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: I understand the question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: PETER GALBRAITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Just broadly, the amount of time that an Ambassador might spend with the head of government or the head of state would depend on the circumstances, both the country you were representing and what was going on in the country where you were serving. In this case, the United States was a principal power concerned with the war. We had a lot of influence with the Croatians. Frankly, all the parties were looking to us as the one power that might be able to help end the war. So I was seeing Tudjman on a very regular basis, dealing with the crisis of the day, whether it was some military action in Bosnia, some action by the Croatian government that we were objecting to, whether it was being briefed about developments but it was because of the war and then because of the peace process, which involved both the process I've described to you with the Krajina Serbs and also the peace process in Bosnia that I was seeing him all the time, alone and also with a steady stream of visitors from Washington as well as from NATO.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: And I must ask you this question: If the Republika Srpska Krajina was not a territory, and it did not have international recognition, nor indeed recognition by your own state, why were you sitting down with it and engaging it in negotiations with a view to peace?

utterances.speaker: PETER GALBRAITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, because there was a war, and it was the goal of my country and of President Clinton to do everything possible to try to end that war. In visiting Knin I was doing so in my capacity as the United States Ambassador to Croatia, visiting a part of the Republic of Croatia, and I met with the local authorities there, the act of meeting with them in no way conferred any recognition of them. I, of course, never used the titles that they themselves used. I never referred to the defendant as President or Mr. Babic as foreign minister or Mr. Mikelic as Prime Minister. But this is something that the United States does in many circumstances, not just in Croatia but in other parts of the world. We do meet with rebels and even those who have themselves proclaimed to have their own state.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: Thank you. For information, you said that Mr. Martic had indicated that he would not meet with you because you had breached protocol by first having meeting or audience with the Minister of Foreign Affairs. Who is that person?

utterances.speaker: PETER GALBRAITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: That would have been Milan Babic. Incidentally, there is, of course, no protocol that would in any diplomatic practice that would suggest that because you meet with the foreign minister, you have in some way offended the president. This was an absurd position that he took.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: I have no further questions and I thank you. I am now going to ask Mr. Whiting to ask any questions arising from the Bench.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. I have no questions to ask.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: And you, Mr. Milovancevic, do you have any questions to put to the witness arising out of the questions coming from the Bench?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I do not have any questions arising from the Bench's questions. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: I'm grateful to you. I believe that that would be the end of the testimony from you and I want to thank you for coming and giving your evidence.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: I want to thank your counsel also.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Your Honour, Mr. Black will be handling the next witness so we are going to do a little switching around here and if I may be excused, as well as Ms. Heather Schildge from the US embassy. I f we could both be excused.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: I had indicated that she could be released and you most certainly can be released.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Your Honours, as soon as the usher returns I'm ready to call our next witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: The next witness is Mr. Stanko Erstic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: Could the witness please take the declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Erstic. Can you hear me and understand me clearly?

utterances.speaker: STANKO ERSTIC
utterances.text: Yes, I can.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: If at any time you don't understand one of my questions please just let me know and I'll try to state it more clearly. Do you understand that?

utterances.speaker: STANKO ERSTIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: First, could you please state your full name for the Court?

utterances.speaker: STANKO ERSTIC
utterances.text: Stanko Erstic.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Mr. Erstic, did you provide a witness statement to this Tribunal in October of 2000?

utterances.speaker: STANKO ERSTIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: And do you remember having a chance to review that statement and certifying its accuracy in June of 2003?

utterances.speaker: STANKO ERSTIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Did you subsequently come to the Tribunal and appear as a witness in the case against Slobodan Milosevic in July of 2003?

utterances.speaker: STANKO ERSTIC
utterances.text: I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Your Honour, Mr. Erstic's prior testimony along with a few associated documents was admitted by your decision of 16 January 2006. The materials have been given exhibit numbers, 392 to 397, and in particular, I would note that Exhibit 392 is the transcript of his testimony in the Milosevic case and Exhibit 396 is his witness statement certified pursuant to Rule 92 bis. Just so it's clear, he appeared as a 92 bis witness in the Milosevic case as well. That's why there is a certified statement in addition to the trial transcript. Now, Your Honours, following the usual practice for a 92 bis witness I'll first read a summary of his evidence. After that I'll have just a couple of questions. Those questions relate to the act and conduct of the accused and that's why they were not tendered pursuant to Rule 92 bis. Before I begin my summary I would merely direct the interest Trial Chamber's attention to page 30 of the atlas which is Exhibit 23. The village of Medvidja which will be discussed appears in grid B-1 just a couple of kilometres north-east of Bruska. I'll now begin the summary.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Black.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. The witness, Stanko Erstic, is a Croat born in the village of Medvidja, Croatia. Relations between Croats and Serbs in his area were reasonably good up until the summer of 1991. However, even before that, local Serbs began gathering in the local bar to sing nationalistic Serb songs, the words to the songs included phrases such as "Milosevic, send us some lettuce. There will be meat because we will be slaughtering Croats." A sign was placed on this bar saying, "Drinks not allowed for Croats and dogs." And Croats in the area were increasingly targeted with hostile remarks from the armed Serb patrons of this bar. This same bar became a hangout for members of Martic's Militia. They mostly wore green camouflage uniforms with a patch on the shoulder saying, militia and SAO Krajina in Cyrillic script. Beginning in 1990, barricades were set up on the roads in this area, around Medvidja and Bruska. As time went on the harassment at these barricades increased and in the summer of 1991 the witness became aware that some people were being arrested at the roadblocks. A few days before the witness was himself detained he saw a local Serb dressed in the uniform of Martic's Militia and carrying an automatic rifle. This person swore at the witness, calling him names and asking him what he was doing. Then this person hit the witness in the chest with the butt of his rifle after which the witness walked away. On the 2nd of October 1991, the witness was detained by two local Serb men who were armed and wearing the uniform of Martic's Militia. They and another local Serb then drove the witness first to Kistanje in a car with licence plates of the Territorial Defence. At Kistanje the witness was held for a short time in a building marked "militia" or police where he saw other militia members. The witness was then taken to Obrovac where he spent the night in a police station that had been taken over by the Serb militia. The next day, still in Obrovac he was interrogated by a Serb police about activities in Medvidja although the witness did not know what they were talking about and eventually they told him he would be taken to Knin. On the next day, the 3rd of October 1991, the witness was taken by two members of Martic's Militia to the old hospital in Knin which was being used as a prison. There, he was detained for one month along with approximately 120 other Croat prisoners, mostly civilians, except for about 20 members of the Croatian National Guard who had been captured in Knin. During his month at the prison, the witness was continually harassed. Beatings and interrogations took place around the clock. Every day the guards would take some detainees out to be beaten, sworn at, taunted and abused. The witness himself received two broken ribs and one cracked rib but other detainees were injured even more severely. The detainees were also forced to do different kinds of work during their detention. The guards at this prison were members of Martic's Militia. While the witness was detained in the prison, Captain Dragan's men and members of the JNA reserve sometimes stayed in a section of the hospital used as a dormitory. The witness frequently saw Captain Dragan's men at the prison. They were not local Serbs and they treated the prisoners better than the others. Captain Dragan's men wore a lighter green uniform than did Martic's Militia and they wore patches with the Serbian flag and the four Cyrillic Ss. On two occasions, the witness saw Ratko Mladic in the prison. On the second of November 1991, the witness was exchanged along with other prisoners. He was picked up from the prison in Knin by members of Mladic's special military police wearing JNA uniforms. The prisoners were first taken on buses to the JNA barracks in Knin where other prisoners boarded the buses. From the barracks, they were taken to the exchange point and about 100 Croats were exchanged for Serb prisoners. After his release the witness stayed in Zadar. He joined the Croatian army in 1993 and he participated in Operation Storm in 1995, although he was not involved in any fighting during that operation. When the witness finally returned to his family home in 1995, his house and about ten others in the hamlet had been destroyed. One of the two village churches had also been mined and damaged. That completes the summary, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Mr. Erstic, I just have two very short topics to ask you about today. First, if we could see on e-court please Exhibit 266? Mr. Erstic in a moment on one of the screens in front of you there will appear an image. We just have to wait for one moment. Mr. Erstic, please look at the image on the screen in front of you and tell the Judges whether you've ever seen a patch like this before.

utterances.speaker: STANKO ERSTIC
utterances.text: Yes. In 1991.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Where did you see a patch similar to this?

utterances.speaker: STANKO ERSTIC
utterances.text: I saw it in my village, and after that in the prison.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Who wore this patch?

utterances.speaker: STANKO ERSTIC
utterances.text: Martic's Militia from Krajina.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Thank you. That's all for that exhibit. Just one more topic, Mr. Erstic. Did you see Milan Martic during October of 1991?

utterances.speaker: STANKO ERSTIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did, in front of the prison, in the yard in front of the prison.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: What was he doing at the time that you saw him?

utterances.speaker: STANKO ERSTIC
utterances.text: He crossed the yard and I saw him as we were unloading some agricultural machines and some food stuff.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Do you remember how he was dressed?

utterances.speaker: STANKO ERSTIC
utterances.text: He wore a camouflage uniform.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Did you notice if he wore any insignia on his uniform?

utterances.speaker: STANKO ERSTIC
utterances.text: The same one, the Krajina Militia.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: When you say the same one, do you mean the one that we just saw on the screen in front of you?

utterances.speaker: STANKO ERSTIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Mr. Erstic, did you know Milan Martic at that time?

utterances.speaker: STANKO ERSTIC
utterances.text: The guards told us that it was him, the militia members who were there told us that.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: I understand that. Just so it's clear, if they had not told you, would you have been able to recognise Milan Martic at that time?

utterances.speaker: STANKO ERSTIC
