utterances.text: Not at the time. I saw him later on TV, and that was that.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Erstic.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Your Honours, I have no more questions in direct examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Black. Mr. Milovancevic?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, it will be Mr. Perovic who will lead the cross-examination. He is my co-counsel.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: Very well. Mr. Perovic, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Erstic.

utterances.speaker: STANKO ERSTIC
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: I suppose you know that I am one of the Defence counsel for Mr. Martic and I will lead the cross-examination as has been envisaged by the rules of the procedure.

utterances.speaker: STANKO ERSTIC
utterances.text: Yes, I'm aware of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: From the summary that has just been read out to us by the Prosecutor, the summary of your statement previously given to the Tribunal, it arises that up to 1990 or 1991 the situation in the area where you resided and the relationship between the Croats and the Serbs were relatively good.

utterances.speaker: STANKO ERSTIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: The situation deteriorated after the referendum in Croatia in the year 1990, a majority of the population voted in favour of the independence of Croatia at that referendum according to you, as you say; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: STANKO ERSTIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: You also say within that context that just like a majority of Croats in 1990 you joined the Croatian Democratic Union; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: STANKO ERSTIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: What governed you in your decision to join the HDZ?

utterances.speaker: STANKO ERSTIC
utterances.text: Nothing in particular, nothing special.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: Maybe I should ask you whether ever before that you belonged to any political party?

utterances.speaker: STANKO ERSTIC
utterances.text: No, never before that. I didn't belong to any party.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: However, you joined the HDZ?

utterances.speaker: STANKO ERSTIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: And you can't say why you joined the HDZ?

utterances.speaker: STANKO ERSTIC
utterances.text: I joined for Croatia, we voted for the HDZ. We wanted to have Croatia as our state, and that was that.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: Within the same context, you also say that after the referendum in 1990, in Rade Pupovac' pub you saw members of the local paramilitaries gathering. That's your wording.

utterances.speaker: STANKO ERSTIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: And you proceed to say that they were all members of Martic's Militia?

utterances.speaker: STANKO ERSTIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: And now, what I would like to know is how come you know that those people who were members of the local paramilitary were also members of Martic's Militia?

utterances.speaker: STANKO ERSTIC
utterances.text: Of course I knew, they had the patches, they wore the insignia featuring the words Martic's Militia. They were armed.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: You believe it is enough for somebody to put on a patch and by doing that they become members of a certain formation?

utterances.speaker: STANKO ERSTIC
utterances.text: They had patches, they were armed, they put up barricades, and they started harassing people, and that was enough.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: Mr. Perovic, just a little bit slower for me, please. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: You were arrested on the 2nd of October 1991?

utterances.speaker: STANKO ERSTIC
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: Who arrested you?

utterances.speaker: STANKO ERSTIC
utterances.text: The Krajina Militia, my next door neighbours, Skoric, Dusan Skoric, Stevo Milanko, and Slobodan Skokna.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: In the summary of your statement, on page 2, you say, "I was arrested by the paramilitary on the 2nd of October 1991."

utterances.speaker: STANKO ERSTIC
utterances.text: Yes, the Krajina Militia.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: You used the word paramilitaries. That's why I'm asking you. Do you make any distinction between the paramilitaries and the militia?

utterances.speaker: STANKO ERSTIC
utterances.text: The paramilitaries were the militia.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: And it is one and the same for you?

utterances.speaker: STANKO ERSTIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You were released on the 2nd of November of the same year, and there was an exchange, wasn't there?

utterances.speaker: STANKO ERSTIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: When you spoke about the moment when you were arrested, you mentioned that you were together with Petar Erstic, a person who bore the same family name.

utterances.speaker: STANKO ERSTIC
utterances.text: Yes, he was my neighbour.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: And you also said that the people from the paramilitary did not show any interest in that person. Why not?

utterances.speaker: STANKO ERSTIC
utterances.text: I don't know. They were just not interested in him. Maybe I was the only person of interest to them.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: Why would that be the case?

utterances.speaker: STANKO ERSTIC
utterances.text: You don't --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter can't hear the witness.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] They said that I had a radio station, which I never saw. I only saw a radio station in the former JNA. That was their explanation.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: I wouldn't go into the details of your stay in prison, save for one thing. You mentioned that two of your ribs were broken and one was fractured; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: STANKO ERSTIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: And during your testimony in the Milosevic case, you said that you did not have any medical documentation about that.

utterances.speaker: STANKO ERSTIC
utterances.text: I beg your pardon, what documentation?

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: Medical documentation?

utterances.speaker: STANKO ERSTIC
utterances.text: Medical documentation? I was sent to treatment. I asked for the documents and they said that they were missing. They were never filed. The first time I was hospitalised was in Rijeka.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: How many detained Croats were there in the prison in Knin where you were?

utterances.speaker: STANKO ERSTIC
utterances.text: About 120 or thereabouts.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: During the exchange that took place on the 2nd of November 1991, how many of you were released from prison?

utterances.speaker: STANKO ERSTIC
utterances.text: 100 or so, 20 remained, those people came from the Lika side.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: The 20 who remained, were they members of the Croatian National Guard Corps?

utterances.speaker: STANKO ERSTIC
utterances.text: There may have been two or three reserve policemen and the rest were civilians, mostly elderly men.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: In other words, during the exchange, 100 Croats were released?

utterances.speaker: STANKO ERSTIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: They were exchanged for 60 Serbs?

utterances.speaker: STANKO ERSTIC
utterances.text: Yes. I suppose so, some 60 or so.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: Who allowed for an exchange of that sort to happen?

utterances.speaker: STANKO ERSTIC
utterances.text: It was the International Red Cross that mediated in that.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: And on the Serb side?

utterances.speaker: STANKO ERSTIC
utterances.text: On the Serb side, Mladic was the one who had the main say.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: Did Martic participate in the exchange in any way?

utterances.speaker: STANKO ERSTIC
utterances.text: I wouldn't know that.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: When you were released from prison in 1993, you joined the Croatian army and you participated in Operation Storm; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: STANKO ERSTIC
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: I don't have any other questions for you, Mr. Erstic. Thank you, Your Honours. This completes my cross-examination of this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Perovic. Mr. Black, do you have any re-examination?

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: None, thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: Any questions, Judge Hoepfel?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: Witness may I ask you once more about the day when you were arrested? You said who arrested you, "the Krajina Militia, my next door neighbours." And then you mentioned four names. They were not exactly clear so can you describe once more the whole scene, who came, who addressed you, and who were -- who was part of that and what was explained to you?

utterances.speaker: STANKO ERSTIC
utterances.text: Let me start with the first things first. Petar Erstic my neighbour called me to help him with some work in the garden. I came over there to help him, and maybe some half an hour or an hour later, from behind a wall, there came two men in camouflage uniforms. They approached us and then I saw that I knew both of them. One of them was Dujo Skoric, also known as Dusan, and Stevo Milanko. I was holding an axe in my hand. I put it on the side at their request, I put it on the ground. They asked me to put my arms in the air. I did that. And they told me, "You're coming with us." I said, "Very well." And they said, "We have things to ask you." I was walking in front of them, they were walking behind me. They didn't say a thing to me while we were walking. Some 300 metres away from that place, they arrested me. On the main road, there was a driver waiting for us. I knew him as well, Slobodan Skokna was his name. They put me in a car, they took me to Kistanje. I stayed in Kistanje for some 20 minutes or half an hour. From Kistanje they took me to Obrovac. I spent the night in Obrovac. On the following morning I was interrogated there. They asked me about a radio station, a radio set which I said I didn't have, and that the only time I ever saw a radio set was in Serbia when I was serving in the JNA. The inspector who interrogated me told me, "Okay, if you don't want to tell us, then we will take to you Knin." Then I told him, "You can do whatever with me. If I don't have that thing, I can't make it up." Maybe 40 minutes or an hour later, they put me in another car and they took me to Knin. When we arrived there, we were -- I was taken to the prison in the old hospital. I had not been aware of the existence of an old hospital there, and then the beatings started, the mistreatment, all sorts of things started after that. And that's how it happened. Then there was this exchange. I was released and at one point I thought I would never see the light of day. What else do you want me to tell you?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: I would like to know if you learned something about who or on whose behalf you were arrested. What authority was it or did you see that just on the insignia and took your own conclusions?

utterances.speaker: STANKO ERSTIC
utterances.text: I didn't know anything else. I only saw their patches and I knew them. They were from my village. We went to school together. Who it was who sent them to arrest me, I really wouldn't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Erstic, I'm going to ask you a few questions. Your ribs that were fractured, were you able to get treatment when you were in prison in respect of that?

utterances.speaker: STANKO ERSTIC
utterances.text: No, no. There were no medicines, there was nothing, no.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: You were not seen by a doctor or a nurse or anybody medical or given any attention whatsoever, having received those injuries?

utterances.speaker: STANKO ERSTIC
utterances.text: Nobody looked after us. One could die sooner than being seen by a doctor.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: Are you still having problems with your ribs or have you recovered?

utterances.speaker: STANKO ERSTIC
utterances.text: I have problems with my back, with my spine, when the weather changes, when there is a south wind or when it rains or when I engage in somewhat heavier labour, then I can feel it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: The other persons who were taken with you, what became of them? Did they remain in prison or what happened?

utterances.speaker: STANKO ERSTIC
utterances.text: I was on my own on that occasion. I was taken there on my own.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: The other persons who were in prison, were they all Croats or were they persons of other nationalities? Were Serbs there?

utterances.speaker: STANKO ERSTIC
utterances.text: There was one Serb from Obrovac. I do not recall his name. He did not want to join either the army or the police and at least that's what he told us and that's why he was imprisoned. And there was also a Croat from Bosnia. I believe that he was from Grahovo.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: Did you see any women at all as prisoners?

utterances.speaker: STANKO ERSTIC
utterances.text: No. There wasn't a single woman there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: When you got back to your village, what did you observe?

utterances.speaker: STANKO ERSTIC
utterances.text: Destroyed, torched, there was not a single roof standing. Everything had been blown up, the church, so that it looked terrible.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: Were there any people there when you got there? Was there inhabitants or --

utterances.speaker: STANKO ERSTIC
utterances.text: There was nobody.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: Thank you. No further questions. Yes, any questions arising out of the questions from the Bench coming from either counsel, Mr. Black, or after you, Mr. Perovic?

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: None from the Prosecution, Your Honour, thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: Mr. Perovic, what about you? What about you, Mr. Perovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just one, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: Yes, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: You mentioned some names, Bosko and Stevo Milanko, Dusan Skoric and Slobodan Skokna as the persons you knew as locals?

utterances.speaker: STANKO ERSTIC
utterances.text: I apologise, Bosko Milanko is a person who hit me with a rifle butt as I was walking to the local store. I never said that he took me to Knin or arrested me.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: I appreciate that. I am interested in something else. You can just wait until I put a question to you. The people whose names you mentioned, were the villagers, that's how you know them?

utterances.speaker: STANKO ERSTIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: Before these events in 1991, who were they engaged in? What was their profession?

utterances.speaker: STANKO ERSTIC
utterances.text: To be honest, they were shepherds, just sheep herders.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have no other questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Perovic. I believe Judge Hoepfel would wish to put a question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: Yes, just for a little clarification. You described this situation of the village when you returned, everything destroyed, as you said, but to be more precise, what really -- what was destroyed and especially I think the Prosecution counsel mentioned two churches, one of them having been mined. Can you be a little more precise?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, there were two churches. One of them was mined and the other was damaged to a great extent. It wasn't completely destroyed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: Mr. Black, Mr. Perovic, anything arising out of that question from Judge Hoepfel.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: No, Your Honour, thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: Mr. Erstic, I want to thank you for coming and giving your evidence. You are now free to leave.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: Mr. Black, we are a little bit past the hour. Would you have another witness to continue with?

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Your Honour, we do not have another witness to continue this week. There were a couple matters that we would like to raise. I think it would take five or ten minutes. I don't know if the preference is to do it now or perhaps come back in half an hour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: You can give an indication but the Chamber certainly intends to come back at 1230 because there is it an outstanding matter that the Chamber had wished to deal with. So you can give an indication the issues that you with wish to raise. Have you -- is Mr. Milovancevic also aware of the issues?

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: No I haven't. He's aware of the issue. I haven't discussed it with him today. It has to do with whether or not the Defence intends to respond to our submissions regarding the evidence of Milan Babic (redacted) (redacted). Those are the two issues I just wanted to raise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: Certainly we had intended to raise the first one and I believe it could be done at 12.30. Is that convenient? Well, certainly, Mr. Milovancevic, you had intended to be here at 12.30 in any event, so we could deal with those issues then and you could have your responses ready.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. That is fine with me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: I look forward to hearing from you. Can we now take the adjournment to 12.30, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: One moment, please, Mr. Black.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Certainly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. It was just a small thing if we could go into private session briefly, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: Yes. We can go into private session, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We are in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes, Mr. Whiting?

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Your Honour, as the court is aware, on April 6, 2006 the Prosecution filed a submission with respect to the evidence of witness Milan Babic setting forth the Prosecution's position in quite detailed form on what we believe should happen with that evidence and why. Under the rule -- under Rule 126 bis of the Rules of Procedure and Evidence the response of the Defence was due on April 20th, 2006. We did not receive either a response nor a motion for an extension of time. On the 21st of April 2006 we filed an application for an order from the Trial Chamber asking that the Defence be ordered to file its response immediately and that in the event the Defence sought an extension of time, that it be granted an extension of time no later than the 27th of April 2006, which is tomorrow. We would submit that the Defence has had more than ample time to write its submissions with respect to this, Milan Babic's evidence. It was exactly seven weeks ago today that the Defence indicated that it could provide its submission within five or six days. Now, later the Defence indicated to us privately that it would wait for our submission and then respond which we found to be perfectly reasonable. However, tomorrow it will have been three weeks since the Prosecution filed its submission. So for those reasons we would ask that the Defence be ordered to file its response to the Prosecution's submission by tomorrow, the 27th of April. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: But you will admit that your motion was quite weighty, not to pre-empt anything but I'm going to ask Mr. Milovancevic to respond.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: I do accept that and I'm -- I really am sort of the last person to try to kind of press absolute, strict adherence to deadlines and for that reason we are agreeable to an extra week. However we do think that the Defence should follow the rules and seek an extension not just let it drift. And if the Defence indicates that it needs a few extra days beyond tomorrow, until Monday, for example, I'm certainly not going to argue about that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Milovancevic, let the Bench, the Chamber, hear from you in respect of the position of the Defence. You had indicated on the 8th, I believe, that we would see a motion forthcoming from you. There has been no motion, in fact, and in the interim the Prosecution has filed its own motion, the OTP, but we have had no response to that either. And the time limit for responding is certainly passed so what will happen and how quickly?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I will answer your question directly. We expect that we will have a response ready by tomorrow or the day after tomorrow at the latest. When the issue of late Milan Babic's testimony was raised for the time, Judge Moloto stated in the order that both the Prosecution and the Defence would give their submissions so we started out -- our point of departure was the fact that we would give our submissions regardless of the Prosecution's submissions. That's why we did not adhere to the time limits although it is true that the Prosecution filed a submission which is quite complex in legal terms and, of course, we have to respond to that as well. And we will do so, we will file that particular response possibly by tomorrow, if not, by the day after tomorrow at the latest.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Milovancevic. I crave the indulgence of both counsel in order for the Trial Chamber to consult.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: You have indicated, Mr. Milovancevic, that by Friday of this week, is it, the relevant responses should be filed and delivered? Is that your position?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's right, Your Honour. That's correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: Can we then make a ruling that by Monday, the 2nd -- sorry, I'm very sorry, one moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: I stand corrected. By Monday, the 1st of May, you will file and deliver the relevant response.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Your Honour, just a small matter. Monday is actually a holiday so perhaps -- it's Queen's Day. It's the Queen's birthday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: Good, sorry. I speak in total ignorance. I overlooked and forgot. You see a smile on my face but I have to remain serious. So then we will be very kind and you're going to get to extra day. Tuesday the 2nd of May, 2006, for the filing of the relevant responses from the Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: Is that okay with you, Mr. Whiting?

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Yes, okay, it is absolutely fine with the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: Fine. And thanks for the correction. Is there any other business? If not, I think we could effectively take our adjournment.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Unfortunately we don't have any other witnesses for this week. Our next witness will be available on Tuesday, May 2nd and I believe we are sitting in the morning. No, or maybe in the afternoon. Don't rely on me for that. We're sitting sometime that day.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: Monday the 1st being effectively a holiday for which I am sure we are all grateful, the sitting of the Chamber will be adjourned until Tuesday the 2nd of May, 2006, in the afternoon, at 2.15, in the relevant courtroom. We will now stand adjourned to that date and that time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
